unitDescription.value: In this unit, students develop foundational woodworking and design skills by producing a timber pencil box from a supplied technical drawing. They learn to safely select and use hand tools and workshop equipment while accurately measuring, marking out, forming timber joints, assembling, sanding and applying a finish to create a durable and functional product. Students also investigate throwaway culture, sustainability and the circular economy, considering how products can be designed for longevity, repair and reduced waste. Using the SBC Year 7 Design Model, students research existing products, generate and refine ideas, produce isometric sketches, evaluate their ideas against design requirements and communicate a final annotated design for an improved, personalised and repairable pencil box.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: Students at St Brendan’s College operate within a diverse learning environment where practical, hands-on application is essential to engagement and skill acquisition. The Year 7–8 Design Technologies curriculum is structured to accommodate varying levels of prior experience with digital systems and manual production techniques. Learning experiences leverage the College’s commitment to vocational pathways and technical literacy, ensuring that students develop fundamental design-thinking skills alongside an appreciation for safety, sustainability, and material performance. Tasks are designed to build student confidence through scaffolded inquiry and iterative prototyping, providing frequent opportunities for students to connect design solutions to authentic, real-world community contexts. Literacy and numeracy support is integrated across all units, ensuring students can effectively communicate design proposals and analyse project data. Teachers differentiate instruction to support the specific needs of the cohort, fostering resilience and independent problem-solving through reflective practice and iterative design cycles that align with the achievement standards of the Australian Curriculum.

description.value: In this assessment, students address the environmental and economic impacts of the 'Throw Away Society' by constructing a durable, long-term storage solution and designing a sustainable iteration. The task requires students to apply technical skills to manufacture a pencil box according to specific design requirements, demonstrating the safe and effective use of appropriate technologies and processes. Concurrently, students use the SBC Year 7 Design Model to develop an improved version of the product that incorporates principles of the Circular Economy. Through a folio of work, students document their design process, justifying their selection of materials and components while communicating innovative ideas through sophisticated design drawings. The final folio evaluates how design modifications can enhance sustainability and product longevity within a modern context.
description.aiNotes:
The quest for new and innovative products combined with profits being made by companies selling as many units as possible has resulted in what is termed a Throw Away Society, where increasingly the cost of repair is more than the cost of replacement. The resultant drain on landfill, construction resources and associated carbon emissions all point to the unsustainability of a Throw Away Society. 

In this unit students will acquire the skills to build and maintain a key item required for the completion of their secondary and tertiary studies as well as produce an improved design that will add to the sustainability and associated financial savings of a pencil box that will last for multiple decades.

Your task is to create a pencil case to the specifications of the design attached, using the materials provided. 

You are also required to design an improved version of the pencil case you have made, incorporating elements of sustainability and the Circular Economy. This design task will be completed as a folio of work, documenting the use of the SBC year 7 Design Model, resulting in a final design drawing.

Assessment Objectives:
•	Develop, modify and communicate design ideas by applying creativity, innovation and skills of increasing sophistication.
•	Work flexibly to effectively and safely test, select, justify and use appropriate technologies and processes to make designed solutions.

activities.title: Workshop Safety Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through the St Brendan's College workshop. Explicitly define key terms: 'Hazard' (an inherent source of potential harm, such as an exposed blade) versus 'Risk' (the likelihood and consequence of injury occurring). Model checking safety equipment: 'Notice how the Emergency Stop is situated at waist height along the perimeter so it can be hit instantly in an emergency.' Walk students past each designated zone without touching live equipment.

activities.questioning:
prompt: Why is the immediate accessibility of an Emergency Stop button critical in a timber production environment?
expected: It allows anyone to instantly cut power to machinery during a mechanical fault or personal emergency, preventing escalation.
prompt: What is the fundamental difference between a hazard and a risk?
expected: A hazard is the source of harm like an exposed blade, whereas risk is the chance and severity of being hurt by it.
activities.scaffolding: Hazard: Any source of potential damage, harm, or adverse health effects (e.g., sharp chisels, airborne timber dust, exposed blades). Risk: The probability that harm will occur from exposure to a hazard. Managed Production Environment: A structured workspace where safety protocols, traffic lanes, and equipment routines actively prevent accidents.

lessons.title: Chisel Safety Induction

activities.title: Chisel Safety Protocols
activities.teacherDoes: Gather students around the central demonstration bench at St Brendan's College workshop. Demonstrate correct chisel handling: two-handed grip (dominant hand on handle supplying controlled forward thrust; non-dominant hand on blade bevel guiding the cut), athletic stance with feet planted wide, and body offset from the line of cut. Model the three non-negotiable rules: both hands behind cutting edge, timber securely clamped in a woodworking vice, and cutting stroke directed away from the body. Show what happens when an unclamped piece moves. Modelled example: 'Notice how my non-dominant hand rests safely behind the steel bolster, and the timber is locked solid in the face vice. If I slip, my fingers are completely out of the line of fire.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration carefully from the safety boundary. In your workbooks, match each chisel safety rule to its correct operational explanation using the provided definition bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Watch the live demonstration closely from the safety boundary. 2. Complete the Chisel Safety Matching table in your workbook. 3. Match each rule in column 1 with its corresponding definition from the bank.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why must both hands always remain behind the cutting edge of a chisel?
expected: If the tool slips through the timber grain suddenly, neither hand is in the path of the sharp bevel.
prompt: Why do we clamp the timber securely in a vice rather than holding it with our non-dominant hand?
expected: Holding timber by hand places fingers directly in the slip trajectory of the blade.
activities.scaffolding: Two-Handed Grip: Dominant hand pushes the wooden handle; non-dominant hand rests on the blade behind the cutting edge to steer. Workpiece Security: Always clamp timber firmly into the bench vice before touching the chisel. Direction of Cut: Never direct a cut toward your torso, arms, or another student.
activities.eLearning: Keep eyes up on the demonstration bench and do not touch any bench tools during the teacher-led demonstration.
activities.transition: Instruct students to move to their allocated workbenches in pairs to inspect their assigned bench chisels under direct supervision.

activities.title: Guided Chisel Handling and Clamping
activities.teacherDoes: Guide the whole class through a step-by-step physical walkthrough at their workbenches. Call out each procedural step: 'Step 1: Don safety glasses. Step 2: Open your bench vice and insert sample pine stock. Step 3: Tighten the vice until timber is rigid. Step 4: Pick up your chisel using the two-handed grip. Freeze for teacher visual check.' Walk the rows inspecting every student's hand placement and body stance before authorising a single light test shave along the end-grain. Model the correct offset stance explicitly, stating: 'Notice how my leading shoulder is turned away from the direct line of travel so that any slip moves harmlessly past my torso.'
activities.studentsDo: Perform each step in sync with the teacher: don safety glasses, clamp pine offcut securely in the bench vice, adopt the two-handed grip with body offset, and execute two controlled light test pairing cuts under visual supervision.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Put on your safety glasses. 2. Secure your scrap timber firmly in your bench vice. 3. Assume the two-handed chisel stance with body offset. 4. Wait for teacher sign-off before performing two light paring cuts. 5. Complete the handling verification checklist in your workbook.
activities.questioning:
prompt: What tactile feedback tells you the timber is clamped tightly enough?
expected: The timber does not shift or vibrate when moderate downward or sideways pressure is applied.
prompt: What happens if your stance is squared directly behind the chisel rather than offset?
expected: If the tool slips, your body momentum will push you directly into the bench or tool edge.
activities.scaffolding: Checklist Verification Steps: 1. Safety glasses secured. 2. Vice tension checked. 3. Stance widened and offset. 4. Dominant hand pushing handle. 5. Non-dominant hand guiding blade bevel behind cutting face. 6. Cutting motion directed strictly away from the body.

activities.title: Tool Management and Maintenance Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that a managed production environment requires active tool maintenance. Display four key woodworking hand tools: a wood chisel, a try-square, a hand plane, and a G-clamp. activities.title: Technical Drawing Conventions
activities.teacherDoes:
Explicitly teach the conventions of technical drawings relevant to the Pencil Case project using the projector. Model how to read the orthographic projection, demonstrating that dimensions indicate true physical size rather than the scale of the printed sheet. Define dimension lines, projection lines, and scale ratios (1:1 and 1:2). Model locating the Face Side and Face Edge reference marks directly on the orthographic plan.

Example script:
'Notice how the dimension lines sit outside the component profile with a clear gap. If these lines touched the object directly, they could be mistaken for actual saw cuts or joinery lines. When you look at the title block, check your scale ratio—if it says 1:2, every millimetre measured on the page must be doubled when marking your Radiata Pine stock.'

activities.questioning:
question: Why must extension lines have a visible gap between the timber boundary and the dimension line?
expected: To prevent extension lines from being misread as physical edges or joinery contours.
question: How does an orthographic projection eliminate visual ambiguity compared to an isometric pictorial sketch?
expected: It isolates distinct 2D views (top, front, end) with exact perpendicular alignments and measurements without perspective distortion.
question: If a component is drawn at 1:2 scale, what arithmetic operation is performed to cut the actual timber workpiece?
expected: Multiply the drawn dimension by 2.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Orthographic Projection: A 2D drawing technique representing different views (front, top, side) of a 3D object at 90-degree angles.
- Dimension Line: A fine unbroken line terminating in arrowheads showing measurable span.
- Extension Line: Thin projection line extending outwards from object contours.
- Scale: The proportional relationship between drawn units and physical millimetres (1:1 = actual size).

activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the 5 foundational joinery terms using physical sample joints and technical diagrams. activities.questioning:
Why does end-grain absorb wood glue faster than edge-grain, and what does this mean for joint strength? Expected: End-grain consists of open hollow tracheid tubes that draw glue away from the joint line like straws, creating a starved and brittle bond.
How does a tolerance deviation of just 1 mm affect a rebate joint during dry-fitting? Expected: A 1 mm gap prevents direct contact between mating faces, eliminating the mechanical interlock and leaving the joint loose and out of square.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
- Butt Joint: A simple corner joint where the end grain of one piece meets the face grain of another without interlocking.
- Rebate Joint: A stepped recess cut along the end or edge of timber providing two mating faces for increased adhesive area.
- Kerf: The width of the groove cut by the saw teeth, determined by blade thickness and tooth set.
- Tolerance: The allowable margin of dimensional error (±0.5 mm) while still maintaining structural integrity.
- Tenon Saw: A stiff-backed saw with fine teeth designed for precise cross-grain joinery cuts.

activities.title: Structural Audit: Butt vs Rebate Joints
activities.teacherDoes: Present physical samples of failed butt joints and intact rebate joints subjected to racking forces. Walk through each structural parameter on the whiteboard: surface contact area, resistance to shear stress, positive alignment, and durability against impact. Demonstrate how the internal 90° shoulder of a rebate joint acts as a mechanical stop that prevents components from slipping during clamping. Model the expected detail level by completing the first row on the board: 'Adhesive Surface Area: Butt joint relies solely on porous end-grain, leading to starved glue lines; rebate joint engages both end-grain and edge-grain faces for maximum bond strength.'
activities.studentsDo: Complete the structural comparison table in the workbook, contrasting butt joints and rebate joints across the 4 key engineering criteria.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the comparison table in your workbook. Detail how the butt joint and rebate joint perform under each structural criterion.
activities.questioning:
question: Why does a rebate joint withstand diagonal racking forces significantly better than a butt joint?
Expected: The rebate joint features an internal timber shoulder that physically blocks lateral movement, transferring racking load into solid wood rather than solely relying on the glue line.
question: When clamping a four-sided box, how does the rebate joint improve assembly accuracy?
Expected: The rebate shoulder provides an automatic registration edge that squares the corners and stops boards sliding when clamp pressure is applied.
activities.scaffolding:
Key comparison concepts:
- Surface contact: Butt = 1 plane (end-grain only); Rebate = 2 planes (end-grain + long-grain face).
- Adhesive bonding: End-grain alone has poor adhesive retention; long-grain face provides high shear strength.
- Mechanical resistance: Butt has zero mechanical interlock; Rebate resists inward racking forces through its shoulder.

activities.transition: With our comparative audit complete, you will now synthesize these engineering principles to justify joint selection for a durable container.

workbookSpec.modelAnswer:

activities.title: Tenon Saw Mechanics & Kerfing Demonstration
activities.teacherDoes: Gather students around the central demonstration bench with safety glasses on. Model the complete setup: securing the timber piece firmly against the bench hook stop, aligning the try-square marked line with the cutting notch, and standing in a balanced side-on stance. Demonstrate the 'kerfing' technique: using backward drawing strokes with the thumb guiding the blade on the waste side of the line to establish a shallow track. Demonstrate cutting at a 45° angle until the far corner depth line is met, then lowering the saw horizontal to complete the shoulder to exact depth. Emphasise keeping the heavy brass back level.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration at the bench. Annotate the technical cutting diagram in your workbook by labelling the 4 sequential procedural checkpoints modelled by the teacher.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the teacher's tenon saw demonstration. In your workbook, annotate the 4 callouts on the cutting diagram with the key procedural rules for stance, kerfing, saw angle, and depth control.
activities.questioning:
Why must the kerf be positioned strictly on the waste side of the marked pencil line? Expected: Because the saw blade has thickness; cutting directly on the line removes timber from the finished component, making the rebate too wide and out of tolerance.
What is the structural role of the brass or steel spine along the top of the tenon saw? Expected: It adds weight to assist cutting pressure and stiffens the thin blade to prevent it from flexing or twisting off a square path.
activities.scaffolding:
Four procedural checkpoints for accurate sawing:
1. Stance & Grip: Stand side-on with index finger pointing forward along the handle for directional control.
2. Workpiece Security: Press the timber firmly into the bench hook fence using the non-dominant hand behind the cut line.
3. Kerf Initiation: Pull backwards 2-3 times with no downward pressure to score an initial channel on the waste side.
4. Angle Progression: Cut at 45° downwards to reach depth at the far edge, then level out the saw to track across the full width.

workbookSpec.title: Sawing Defect & Remediation Analysis
workbookSpec.prompt: Diagnose the 3 most common sawing errors and record the workshop remediation technique to correct each fault.

Row 3: Cause = Unsupported grain at the exit edge or excessive downward force on the push stroke. Remediation = Clamp scrap backing timber or ease forward pressure as the blade exits the wood fibres.

activities.title: Chisel Paring Demonstration & Practice
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate at the front bench how to safely pare the waste out of the rebate joint cut in Lesson 2. Clamp the workpiece securely in the woodworking vice with the waste projecting upward. Emphasise the golden rule: both hands must remain behind the cutting edge at all times (one hand wrapping the neck to control depth, one on the handle driving the cut). Model horizontal paring: bevel facing up, working in thin stepped shavings from the outer corner towards the shoulder line. Demonstrate checking bed flatness using the edge of a steel rule.

activities.questioning:
prompt: Why must you pare the timber in thin shavings rather than attempting to split the entire waste block out in one cut?
expected: Forcing a large cut follows the natural timber grain, which can split downward below the gauge line and ruin the joint bed.
prompt: Why is the chisel bevel kept facing upwards when paring horizontally along the rebate bed?
expected: The flat back of the chisel registers against the timber surface to maintain a level horizontal cut, preventing the blade from digging into the joint floor.

1. Secure timber in the vice with the rebate horizontal and waist-height.
2. Both hands behind the cutting edge: non-dominant hand on blade for control, dominant hand on handle.
3. Make light slicing cuts working from the outside edge towards the shoulder.
4. Stop exactly at the marking gauge depth line.
5. Test bed flatness with the narrow edge of a steel rule.

activities.title: Evaluating Rebate Joint Tolerance
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through evaluating their pared rebate joint using a structured 5-point continuum. Model how to measure joint gap width with a steel rule and inspect shoulder squareness against a engineer's square. Show examples of joints rated 1 (loose/dished), 3 (functional but minor gaps), and 5 (seamless fit within ±0.5 mm tolerance). Instruct students to apply the continuum scale in their workbooks and justify their rating using precise QCAA workshop terminology such as 'grain tearing', 'bed flatness', and 'shoulder registration'.

activities.questioning:
question: What causes a joint bed to become 'dished' or hollow in the centre during paring?
expected: Applying too much downward pressure on the centre of the blade, causing the chisel to scoop wood out below the perimeter gauge lines.
question: How does an uneven rebate bed affect glue line strength when clamped?
expected: Glue fills the gap rather than wood fibres bonding directly; standard PVA glue has low tensile strength in thick gaps, leading to joint failure under load.
activities.scaffolding:
Continuum descriptor anchors:
- 1: Loose fit (>1.5 mm gaps), dished bed, end-grain torn.
- 3: Snug fit (0.5-1.0 mm gaps), minor light visible under rule, slight rounding at shoulder.
- 5: Perfect mechanical fit (<0.5 mm tolerance), completely light-tight, flat bed, 90° shoulder.

activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the unit's core theoretical pillar: moving beyond single-use fabrication. Define the four technical terms explicitly on the whiteboard. activities.questioning:
question: Why does end-grain absorb glue faster than face-grain?
expected: End-grain acts like hollow drinking straws (open tracheids/capillaries) which suck adhesive away from the joint interface, potentially causing a dry joint.
question: What happens to a joint if excessive clamping pressure is applied?
expected: It causes 'glue starvation', where the majority of the adhesive is squeezed out, leaving insufficient bonding medium between the timber faces to sustain structural integrity.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions for reference: 1. PVA: A water-based aliphatic emulsion that penetrates wood pores to create a mechanical interlocking bond. 2. Capillary Action: The movement of liquid adhesive into the microscopic cellular structure of timber. 3. Uniform Pressure: Evenly distributed clamping force that closes gaps without starving the joint of adhesive. 4. Racking: Distortion where a rectangular frame skews into a parallelogram because opposing corners are not square.

activities.title: Generative Assembly Troubleshooting Analysis
activities.teacherDoes: Transition students to the diagnostic phase by presenting three photographic case studies of common assembly failures: Racked frames, glue-starved joints, and clamp bruising. If you see a racked frame, the time to fix it is now.' Model one example on the board: 'For a glue-starved joint, the root cause is often excessive pressure squeezing all adhesive out. The rectification is to ensure the joint is flush during dry-clamping, then applying moderate, even pressure during final assembly.'

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
Scenario A: Cause - Clamping pressure was applied unevenly or square was not verified during initial glue-up. Rectification - Position a sash clamp across the longer diagonal (220mm) and apply gentle, incremental tension until both diagonals measure 216mm; verify squareness with a framing square before the adhesive sets.
Scenario B: Cause - Excessive clamping pressure forced all adhesive out of the interface (starved joint), or excessive drying time prior to clamping. Rectification - Ensure joints fit flush via dry-clamping; apply a consistent, thin film of PVA to mating surfaces; clamp with moderate, uniform pressure within 5 minutes of application.
Scenario C: Cause - Rigid steel clamp jaws were applied directly against the soft radiata pine surface. Rectification - Always insert sacrificial scrap timber blocks (cauls) between the steel clamp jaws and the finished workpiece surface to distribute clamping pressure and prevent indentation.

4. Surface Protection: Timber cauls must be used at every clamp jaw interface to prevent indentation marks.

activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the 'diagonals check' procedure. Explain that measuring the diagonals is the primary method to verify squareness in timber frame construction. Model the physical check: 'Apply light clamping pressure until the joints close. Place your steel rule diagonally across the internal corners. If diagonal A is 450mm and diagonal B is 452mm, the frame is out of square by 2mm. Tighten the sash clamp pressure on the side corresponding to the long diagonal to pull the frame into square. If you see light through a try-square placed against the inside corner, the joint is not perfectly 90 degrees; adjust clamp placement.'

5. Verify corner squareness with a try-square.
6. Request teacher sign-off before applying glue.

What is the physical cause of a sash clamp causing the box to 'rack' or twist? Expected: Uneven pressure distribution or non-parallel clamp jaws; the user must re-centre the clamp or adjust the head/tail stock placement.
Why must we record the difference between diagonal A and B? Expected: To quantify 'squareness'. If the difference exceeds 1mm, the box is structurally misaligned, which will lead to gaps in finished joints and instability.

activities.questioning:
question: Why do vertical lines in isometric projection remain strictly vertical while receding horizontal lines are drawn at 30 degrees?
expected: Isometric projection maintains equal foreshortening along all three primary axes (120° apart) to prevent perspective distortion, requiring strict adherence to these specific angles.
question: Why must the initial crate be drawn using faint 2H construction lines?
expected: Construction lines establish proportion and scale within the bounded volume. They must remain faint to ensure the final HB outlines (the actual object design) remain the dominant visual feature.
activities.scaffolding:
Isometric Convention Guide:
- Vertical Axis: 90° to the horizontal baseline.

activities.title: Modelled Putty Application and Micro-Planing
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate at the demonstration bench with safety glasses on. Show the two-stroke putty knife technique: press putty firmly into the nail hole at 45 degrees to pack the void, then hold the blade at 15 degrees to shear excess cleanly, leaving a 1 mm raised mound. Next, demonstrate tuning the sliding lid: show how to inspect the groove for glue beads, use a micro-plane along the tongue parallel to the grain, taking whisper-thin shavings, and test fit after every two passes. Explicitly highlight holding timber firmly in the woodwork vice with protective cork jaws. Modelled example: 'Notice how the 45-degree angle forces the timber filler deep into the grain pores. When I switch to 15 degrees, I am shearing off the bulk so I don't spend excess time sanding later.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration from behind the workshop safety line. Note the angle transitions of the putty knife and the light, controlled stroke of the micro-plane.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the demonstration: 1. Watch the 45-degree packing stroke followed by the 15-degree shearing stroke with the putty knife. 2. Observe how the micro-plane is used with the timber grain to ease lid friction.
activities.questioning:
Why do we change the blade angle from 45 degrees to 15 degrees when applying timber putty?
Expected: The 45-degree angle forces putty deep into the timber pores, while the 15-degree angle slices away excess putty cleanly to minimise subsequent sanding.
Why must we test-fit the lid after every two light strokes of the micro-plane rather than planing heavily?
Expected: Removing too much timber causes the lid to rattle and derail, permanently ruining the tight manufacturing tolerance.

Technique cues:
- Putty blade: 45° push to fill -> 15° draw to level proud.
- Micro-plane: Clamp lid in vice -> plane with the grain -> test fit every 2 passes.
- Quality standard: 1 mm overfill on holes; lid slides smoothly with one-finger push without falling out when tilted.

activities.teacherDoes: Introduce technical criteria used to evaluate sustainable timber products under the circular economy framework. Display diagrams showing linear lifecycle (take-make-waste) versus circular lifecycle (make-use-repair-recycle). Contrast permanent joint bonding against modular demountability: 'When designing your modifications, adding features like internal dividers or custom lids creates trade-offs between internal storage capacity, manufacturing complexity, and repairability.' q: How does designing a modular lid increase a timber product's lifespan compared to a permanently glued lid?
Expected: If the lid cracks or wears down, a modular component can be individually replaced or repaired without discarding the entire box.
q: What is the design trade-off between adding multiple internal stationery compartments and the box's usable capacity?
Expected: Dividers consume internal volume and add manufacturing complexity, reducing space available for larger drawing instruments.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
1. Demountability: The design quality enabling a product to be disassembled cleanly without damaging components, allowing repair or material recycling.
2. Product Longevity: The ability of a product to resist physical wear, structural fatigue, and aesthetic obsolescence over an extended service life.
3. Functional Capacity: The volume of usable interior storage available for intended tools relative to the external dimensions of the product.
4. Design Complexity: The degree of difficulty, number of parts, and manufacturing precision required to produce and assemble a product.

activities.questioning:
q: Why does excessive manufacturing complexity often undermine circular economy goals for secondary students?
Expected: Complex parts with fragile, multi-layered joints are more likely to fail during fabrication or use, and are significantly harder for an end-user to disassemble or repair.
q: How does selecting solid native timber over synthetic composites support circular material flows?
Expected: Solid timber can be planed down, refinished, composted, or remanufactured at end-of-life, whereas synthetic composites bonded with resins cannot be easily separated or recycled.

- Standardisation: Standard dimensions make replacement parts simple to fabricate.

activities.title: Abrasive Material Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Display cross-sectional microscopic slides of aluminium oxide particles and pine grain cells. Deliver the explicit definitions of key terminology: grit number, backing substrate, friability, and grain raising. Model how friable grains shear under mechanical friction: 'When aluminium oxide grains fracture under pressure, they create micro-cleavages that expose new razor-sharp cutting facets instead of polishing dull edges.' Emphasise that grit measures particle count per square linear mesh opening.
activities.studentsDo: Read the term column in the workbook table. Review the scrambled definition bank and write the corresponding definition into the blank Match cell for all four terms.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each abrasive term in column 1 to its technical definition from the bank below. Write the matching definition clearly into the Match column.
activities.questioning:
Why does a low grit number like 80 indicate larger mineral particles? Expected: Grit refers to the mesh gauge per square inch, so fewer, larger particles fit through coarse mesh screens.
What occurs physically to wood cell walls during 'grain raising'? Expected: Moisture penetrates severed wood cell walls, causing cell lumens to swell and stand upright above the flat surface.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
1. Grit Number: Density rating of abrasive mineral particles per linear inch of sizing mesh (lower number = larger mineral particles).
2. Backing Substrate: Flexible paper, cloth, or vulcanised fibre base carrying the bonded abrasive minerals.
3. Friability: The mechanical property of abrasive grains to micro-fracture under friction, continually renewing cutting facets.
4. Grain Raising: Expansion of crushed timber tracheid cells when exposed to water or moisture, producing raised, rough fibres.

activities.transition: Now that we have defined how abrasive minerals cut, let us examine how changing grit grades systematically removes machining marks without destroying the surface.

activities.title: Grit Sequence Mechanics
activities.teacherDoes: Sketch three scratch profiles on the whiteboard: deep 80-grit V-grooves, shallower 120-grit grooves that level off the peaks, and 240-grit micro-scratches. Explain the mechanics of scratch replacement: 'Abrasives do not erase scratches; smaller abrasives replace deeper gouges with microscopic furrows until surface reflection is uniform.' Demonstrate what happens if 120-grit is skipped: the 240-grit abrasive merely polishes the bottom of 80-grit troughs without levelling the timber face.
activities.studentsDo: Track the whiteboard progression and complete the cloze passage in the workbook by selecting the correct technical terms from the word bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the numbered blanks in your workbook cloze passage using the terms provided in the word bank.
activities.questioning:
question: What visual defect remains if a student jumps directly from 80-grit to 240-grit sandpaper?
expected: Deep primary scratches remain visible under clear coat finishes because 240-grit particles cannot reach the bottom of 80-grit trenches.
question: Why must sanding strokes always travel parallel to the longitudinal grain?
expected: Perpendicular strokes cut across hollow timber fibres, leaving torn cross-grain tears that darken irreversibly when stained or sealed.
activities.scaffolding:
Core Sequence Rules:
1. 80-grit: Bulk stock removal, joint flush-levelling, glue squeeze-out clean-up.
2. 120-grit: Intermediate levelling, removing 80-grit scratch pattern.
3. 240-grit: Pre-finish polishing, smoothing cell walls for clear varnish application.
4. Grain alignment: Long strokes with grain lines, never perpendicular.

activities.title: Sanding Block Setup & Grain Inspection
activities.teacherDoes: Gather students around the central demonstration bench. Model how to fold and wrap a quarter-sheet of 80-grit sandpaper around a cork-faced wooden sanding block with taut corners. Demonstrate how holding loose sandpaper in the fingers rounds over sharp edges and hollows soft earlywood rings. Inspect an assembled pencil box under direct raking light, tracing the longitudinal grain with a finger and highlighting dried glue beads and tear-out along the rebate joint. Model explicit responses: 'Notice how Callout 1 points directly along the longitudinal grain vector to ensure our sanding strokes never cut across timber cell structures.'
activities.studentsDo: Examine the faces of your assembled timber pencil box. On your workbook layout diagram, record the callout numbers matching the grain direction, glue residue, machine marks, and rebate joint boundary.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine your timber pencil box. Complete the numbered callouts on your workbook diagram to identify longitudinal grain direction, dried glue, machining marks, and rebate joint seams.
activities.questioning:
Why does a flat sanding block maintain surface accuracy better than bare hand pressure? Expected: The rigid block bridges across high and low spots to level the surface, whereas fingers compress into softer growth rings and create an uneven, wavy surface.
What visual indicator shows that glue residue has not been fully removed from a timber joint? Expected: The adhesive appears as a glossy, non-porous patch that repels timber dust and prevents the abrasive from cutting into the wood fibres beneath.
activities.scaffolding:
Inspection Terms:
1. Longitudinal Grain: Alignment of wood tracheid cells running along board length.
2. Glue Residue: Cured PVA adhesive on surface pores requiring 80-grit levelling.
3. Machining Scuffs: Circular or transverse blade indentations across timber face.
4. Edge Chamfer: Controlled bevel on box rim to avoid splintering.

activities.title: Executing Progressive Sanding
activities.teacherDoes: Monitor the workshop floor as students sand. Ensure students use long, even strokes parallel to the grain. Intervene immediately if cross-grain circular scrubbing is observed. Circulate with a raking inspection light to examine timber boxes. Prompt students: 'Wipe all dust away with a microfibre cloth before opening your 120-grit paper. Stray 80-grit grains trapped under 120-grit paper will score deep trenches into your pine.' Sign off inspection boxes when students demonstrate defect-free surfaces.

activities.questioning:
question: What does a tactile check with your fingertips reveal that your eyes might miss under overhead fluorescent lighting?
expected: Fingertips detect subtle height differences across joint seams and localized ridges that visual inspections under diffuse light overlook.
question: Why must surface timber dust be completely cleared before switching from 120-grit to 240-grit?
expected: Coarser loose mineral grains from the 120-grit paper will drag across the face, gouging random scratches into the refined 240-grit surface.

- 80-Grit: Remove joint offsets, glue beads, and machine ripples. Surface feels toothy/rough.
- 120-Grit: Eliminate all 80-grit linear scratch marks. Surface feels uniform and flat.
- 240-Grit: Eliminate 120-grit scratches, buff wood cell fibres. Surface feels silky smooth with no visible scratches under raking light.

activities.title: Quality Assurance Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define Quality Assurance (QA) versus Quality Control (QC) within timber manufacturing. Delivery script: 'Quality Assurance refers to the systematic checks and processes carried out during production to ensure defects do not occur. Quality Control is the inspection of the completed artefact against the supplied technical drawing. When timber components deviate from the drawing, gaps create localized stress points, compromising structural integrity.' Model the three key vocabulary terms on the whiteboard, highlighting how adherence to technical tolerance (+/- 1.0 mm) prevents joint failure.

activities.questioning:
Why is verifying tolerance throughout timber assembly more effective than only inspecting the finished box? Expected: Checking components early allows for rectification before glue sets or joints are permanently fixed, preventing material wastage.
How does a loose joint fit impact the durability and circular economy lifecycle of the pencil box? Expected: A loose fit weakens the adhesive bond under shear stress, causing premature structural failure and forcing early disposal rather than long-term use.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
- Tolerance: The permissible limit of variation in a physical dimension (+/- 1.0 mm).
- Structural Integrity: The ability of an assembled timber structure to withstand operational load without deformation or joint fracture.
- Surface Finish: The tactile smoothness and visual uniformity of timber grain, free from tear-out, cross-grain scratches, and adhesive bleed.

activities.title: Refinement Techniques and Chamfering Demonstration
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate corrective finishing techniques on a sample box with common defects: a proud rebate joint and sharp external arrises. Delivery script: 'To bring proud joinery flush without gouging adjacent timber, support the file flat across both members and stroke forward with light, even pressure along the grain. To remove sharp arrises and prevent splintering, hold a fine-cut bastard file at precisely 45 degrees to establish a uniform 1 mm chamfer along the top perimeter. Always use a cork sanding block when working flat faces; fingers create depressions that reflect light unevenly once finished.' Model the 4 target zones on the projected diagram.

activities.questioning:
question: Why must filing always be executed with forward, pushing strokes rather than scrubbing back and forth?
expected: File teeth cut exclusively on the forward stroke; dragging backward dulls the teeth and tears timber grain.
question: What is the mechanical purpose of applying a 1 mm chamfer to the top external edges of the box?
expected: Chamfering removes fragile sharp arrises (corners), preventing splintering and impact damage during daily handling.

3. Lid Slide Groove -> Gentle edge easing with folded 240-grit paper to eliminate binding.
4. Face Grain -> Planar sanding with cork block using 240-grit paper in the direction of the grain.

activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the evaluative criteria required for secondary design technology portfolios at St Brendan's College. Delivery script: 'In design evaluation, we avoid descriptive storytelling like 'I made a box and it looked good.' activities.teacherDoes: Deliver explicit instruction contrasting the linear 'take-make-waste' model against circular product design. Script: 'In modern consumer culture, products like plastic pencil cases are designed for planned obsolescence—when a clip snaps, the entire case enters landfill. activities.questioning:
Why does designing a product for repairability require greater manufacturing precision than designing a disposable product? Expected: Replaceable parts must meet exact tolerances so that new replacement components fit accurately into existing assemblies years later.
How does using solid timber rather than composite engineered boards (like MDF) support biological cycling in a circular economy? Expected: Untreated natural timber is biodegradable and can safely return nutrients to the soil or be repurposed, whereas resin-bonded MDF produces toxic dust and cannot be composted.

- 'lifecycle' refers to the journey from raw resource to end-of-life.
